World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On JAL's Boeing 787-9, you'll be seated in the Sky Suite — a fully flat, forward-facing seat with a sliding door for privacy. The seat converts to a 186-cm flat bed with a proper mattress pad and duvet. The personal screen is one of the largest in the sky at 23 inches.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool shows JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

Not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

JAL Sky Suite business class features angled lie-flat or fully lie-flat seats depending on the aircraft, with a privacy shell, excellent Japanese cuisine, attentive service, and premium amenity kits. The service quality is consistently praised as among the best in the industry. On 777-300ER and 787 aircraft, the product competes with top-tier offerings from Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

Golding is only 20 though, and he’s out on his first senior loan with League Two side Shrewsbury Town. The Foxes will have hoped he could find regular minutes with Gavin Cowan’s side, but that has not been the case.

Also: How Chrome warns you about suspicious websites now

X (formerly Twitter) user, Leopeva64, posted a short video and several still images showcasing a potential new feature in Chrome Canary, which Google uses to test new Chrome web tools and features. The posts show the search bar pinned to the top of the settings menu for instant access. By entering the name of the submenu or feature you want to access, the new search bar could save a lot of time normally spent clicking around, trying to remember exactly where it’s located.

In Chrome Canary, Google is testing removing the scroll arrows that let you automatically scroll to reveal hidden items when you hover over them in the 3-dot menu. According to Leopeva64, other possible new features include a visual update that groups similar menu options into tiles for faster navigation of your most-accessed settings, as well as pinning the menu footer to keep it visible as you click through.

Chrome Extensions is also up for a possible refresh with a move to a dedicated submenu called Manage Skills to help keep all of your installed extensions organized and make it easier to remove ones that are no longer needed.

Also: How to take full-page screenshots in Chrome on any device – it’s easy and free

Google Lens may get a new submenu, called “Ask Google about this page,” for searching for items you see across an entire page, not just in a single image.

There’s no official word yet on when these features will leave Canary’s testing environment and become available in the regular Chrome menu. I’ve reached out to Google for a comment, but at the time of writing, I have not received a response.

« J’ai accepté cette proposition avec beaucoup d’enthousiasme » : Rafael Nadal prend du galon au Real Madrid !

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Le conseil d'administration du Real Madrid a officialisé ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 la proposition d'intégrer Rafael Nadal au sein de son Conseil d’administration. Une arrivée majeure pour le club de la capitale et son président Florentino Pérez, qui doit désormais être soumise au vote des socios.

Réuni ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, le conseil d'administration du Real Madrid a convenu de soumettre à l'assemblée générale des socios la ratification de la nomination de Rafael Nadal Parera comme nouveau membre de son Conseil d’administration. Cette proposition intervient en application de l'article 46 des statuts sociaux du club madrilène. Âgé de 40 ans et retraité des courts depuis 2024, le champion espagnol aux 22 tournois du Grand Chelem, dont un record de 14 victoires à Roland-Garros, franchit ainsi une étape institutionnelle majeure. Une figure emblématique du sport mondial au service du club de son cœur.

D'ailleurs, l'ancienne star du tennis n'arrive pas en terre inconnue dans la capitale espagnole, puisqu'il est socio d'honneur du Real Madrid et porte le numéro de socio 67 778. Dans un communiqué officiel publié ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, l'institution madrilène a salué cette future arrivée : « Le Conseil d’administration du Real Madrid CF, réuni ce mercredi 4 novembre, a décidé de soumettre à l’Assemblée générale des membres délégués la ratification de la nomination de Rafael Nadal Parera, membre numéro 67 778 de notre club, en tant que nouveau membre du Conseil d’administration. Rafael Nadal, membre honoraire du Real Madrid, est l’une des plus grandes légendes de l’histoire du sport et l’un des athlètes espagnols les plus admirés et reconnus au monde. Pour le Real Madrid et pour tous les supporters madrilènes, c’est une grande fierté qu’une figure de son envergure sportive et humaine, une référence du sport espagnol et mondial, rejoigne notre conseil d’administration et contribue, depuis cette position à responsabilité, au présent et à l’avenir de notre club ».

Dans la foulée de cette annonce, Rafael Nadal a réagi publiquement sur ses réseaux sociaux pour partager son sentiment, en publiant une photo de lui enfant portant le maillot du Real Madrid et en remerciant le dirigeant merengue. « Je tiens à remercier le président Florentino Pérez et le conseil d’administration de m’avoir proposé de rejoindre le conseil d’administration du Real Madrid. J’ai accepté cette proposition avec beaucoup d’enthousiasme, l’envie d’apprendre et de m’investir autant que possible », a confié l'Espagnol.

Cet engagement clarifie la place de l'Espagnol au sein de la Maison Blanche. Plus tôt au cours de l'année 2026, Rafael Nadal avait déjà démenti sur ses réseaux sociaux les rumeurs l'associant à une éventuelle candidature à la présidence du club. Pas question de viser le sommet de l'organigramme pour l'instant. Il s'agit uniquement d'un rôle d'administrateur, où il entend apporter sa contribution au présent et au futur du Real Madrid.

Toutefois, l'intégration de la légende espagnole n'est pas encore définitivement actée. La ratification de sa nomination sera formellement soumise au vote des socios délégués lors d'une assemblée générale extraordinaire convoquée le samedi 21 novembre 2026. Cette réunion se tiendra au pavillon de basket de la Ciudad Real Madrid, immédiatement après l'assemblée générale ordinaire, avec pour unique point à l'ordre du jour la validation de l'entrée de Rafael Nadal.

Sur le plan sportif, le Real Madrid dispute ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 à 18h45 un match contre l'AEK Athènes à l'Allwyn Arena pour la 4e journée de Ligue des champions. Les Madrilènes enchaîneront ensuite avec un déplacement en Liga contre le Valence CF à Mestalla, programmé le samedi 7 novembre 2026 à 21h00.

ARRAY Technologies and Shoals plan to merge companies

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Solar tracker and racking manufacturer ARRAY Technologies and electrical balance of systems (eBOS) provider Shoals Technologies have initiated a stock-for-stock merger to combine both companies.

“This transaction represents a compelling opportunity to create meaningful value for customers of both ARRAY and Shoals by bringing together our complementary strengths. Although structural and electrical systems must operate seamlessly together in the field, they have historically been designed and sourced through separate channels. This combination changes that. Together, we expect to deliver a differentiated, technically integrated and interoperable platform that simplifies project execution, enhances project economics and accelerates innovation for customers,” said Kevin Hostetler, CEO of ARRAY.

According to the press announcement, ARRAY will be Shoals’ parent company after the transaction, with Shoal’s CEO Brandon Moss assuming the role as CEO for the overall company. ARRAY’s CEO Kevin Hostetler will transition to a special advisor role for the company.

“Today marks an important milestone for Shoals, ARRAY and the customers we serve. By bringing together two highly complementary businesses with experienced teams, we are creating an integrated platform with broader capabilities, deeper customer relationships and a stronger foundation for long-term growth. We believe the combined company will be positioned to better service customers, deliver more innovative and integrated solutions, realize meaningful synergies and pursue expansion opportunities across the solar value chain, data center markets and beyond,” said Brandon Moss, CEO of Shoals.

The companies plan to create packaged warranties across their structural and eBOS products. As manufacturers, both ARRAY and Shoals have supplied their products to solar and energy storage projects globally.

ARRAY is known for producing single-axis solar trackers that use an inter-row rotating mechanism. Over the years, the company has iterated on its trackers to use multi- and dual-row architectures, and to be deployed on undulating topographies. These rotating solar structures are supported with proprietary tracker operations software with considerations such as shading and hail and wind stowing.

Shoals manufactures combiner boxes and cable management solutions for multi-market scale solar and energy storage projects, as well as data centers.

“Having had the privilege of serving as chairman of both ARRAY and Shoals, I have seen firsthand the complementary products, talented teams and shared commitment to customers offered by both companies,” said Brad Forth, chairman of the board of directors of ARRAY and Shoals. “Together, ARRAY and Shoals are well positioned to deliver enhanced value to customers, shareholders and employees. I also want to thank Kevin for his leadership and important contributions to ARRAY, as well as his valuable insights as he transitions to a Special Advisor role. I look forward to continuing to work with Brandon, who brings proven leadership, deep industry expertise and strategic vision to lead the combined company in this next phase of growth.”

Both ARRAY’s and Shoals’ boards have reportedly unanimously approved the merger, with Forth abstaining from the vote. The merger is expected to complete in Q1 2027.

While not mergers, ARRAY Technologies has been acquiring companies producing technologies complementary to solar trackers. Last year, ARRAY acquired fixed-tilt racking and foundations manufacturer APA Solar Racking, and just acquired Affordable Wire Management, a cable management solutions provider, this past September.

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

PANAMA CITY, November 4, 2026 — Bitbase today launched ORIGIN, the first season of its Bitbase Points program, which is designed to reward sustained participation over time. Over the 26-week season, which ends on May 4, 2027, Bitbase will distribute 1,000,000 points each week, allocated daily according to each participant’s contribution.

Each participant’s contribution is drawn from four sources: trading, assets held on Bitbase, consistent activity and referrals. Consistent activity is counted as a separate source, so continued participation from day to day adds to a user’s contribution. All eligible users, whether new to Bitbase or already active on the platform, are enrolled automatically.

For each new user referred directly, the referrer receives an additional 25% of that user’s contribution. The new user’s own points are not affected.

Participants will also receive a Trading Identity card, a shareable summary of their trading style. The first cards will be issued on November 9, with new cards following each Monday for the remainder of the season.

Existing users begin with points already credited

Before the season began, Bitbase credited points to eligible existing users based on their earlier activity on the platform. As a result, these users enter ORIGIN with their prior activity already reflected in their points and ranking.

On November 2, the exchange introduced Bitbase 2.0, updating its brand, app and website under the statement “Market Flows. We Focus.” ORIGIN is the first program to put that statement into practice. While markets move continuously, Bitbase has chosen to assess participation across months rather than individual moments.

“We designed ORIGIN for users who participate consistently, not only during the busiest periods in the market,” said Nicholas Lo, Chief Business Officer at Bitbase. “Over a six-month season, that consistency carries weight. Our responsibility is to make sure every contribution is credited, from the first day of the season to the last.”

Points and rankings are available in the Bitbase app and at bitbase.com/points.

Bitbase is a digital asset exchange serving individual and institutional users worldwide, with products spanning Spot, Futures, TradFi and Earn. Bitbase aims to give users a stable and straightforward trading experience, in line with its brand statement, “Market Flows. We Focus.” Learn more at bitbase.com.

Easier installation and improved thermal conductivity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Thermal Grizzly has announced the PhaseSheet PTM Pro, an improved version of its popular phase-changing thermal pad. According to the manufacturer, the new thermal pad offers increased thermal conductivity alongside a redesigned carrier film that makes the PhaseSheet PTM Pro easier to handle and install. While this may seem like a relatively minor change, the new carrier film is designed to peel away more easily from both sides, reducing the risk of tearing the sheet during installation.

Like the original PhaseSheet PTM, the Pro version uses a phase-changing material that alters its physical properties depending on the temperature. At room temperature, the sheet remains solid, much like a conventional thermal pad. However, at temperatures above 45°C, the material transitions into a very low-viscosity liquid that behaves similarly to thermal paste.

This phase-changing behavior helps minimize the pump-out effect commonly associated with traditional thermal paste. Pump-out occurs when thermal paste gradually moves out from between a heatsink and a GPU die or CPU IHS due to repeated thermal expansion and contraction of the contacting surfaces. Over time, this can reduce the amount of thermal paste covering the contact area and potentially degrade cooling performance.

The PhaseSheet PTM Pro is also reusable and electrically non-conductive, meaning it can be safely used on components without an IHS, including mobile CPUs, GPUs, and other internal components such as memory and storage. According to a performance graph shared by Thermal Grizzly, the new PhaseSheet PTM Pro outperforms several popular thermal pastes and thermal pads in controlled testing. Using a 30 x 30mm contact area, 300N of mounting force (48 PSI), and a 240W heat load, the PhaseSheet PTM Pro recorded a temperature difference of 5.83°C, the lowest among all the tested materials. This puts it ahead of the KryoSheet (6.13°C), Duronaut Pro (6.29°C), and the original PhaseSheet PTM (6.36°C).

The PhaseSheet PTM Pro can be purchased through Thermal Grizzly's website for $23.28 per 40 x 40mm sheet. That's considerably more expensive than the original PhaseSheet PTM, which costs $13.92 for a larger 50 x 40mm sheet.

Panama City, November 4, 2026 — Bitbase today launched ORIGIN, the first season of its new Bitbase Points program. Ahead of the launch, the digital asset exchange credited points to eligible users who had been trading on the platform, so their past activity counts from day one. The season runs for 26 weeks, until May 4, 2027, with 1,000,000 points distributed each week.

ORIGIN is also the first part of Bitbase 2.0 to reach users directly. Bitbase unveiled 2.0 on November 2, with an upgraded app and website and a new brand identity built around the statement “Market Flows. We Focus.” The idea is that markets will always move, and Bitbase chooses to focus on what lasts for its users. ORIGIN applies the same thinking to participation. Rather than rewarding a single burst of activity, it looks at what users do day after day over six months and credits the contribution they make across that period.

Bitbase built ORIGIN around what users already do on the exchange. Eligible users, new or existing, are enrolled automatically, with no separate registration. Points are allocated daily based on each participant’s contribution, which draws on four sources: trading, assets held on Bitbase, consistent activity and referrals. Because consistency is one of those sources, steady participation adds up over the course of the season.

ORIGIN also rewards users who bring others to Bitbase. A referrer receives an additional 25% of the contribution of each new user they refer directly, while the new user’s own contribution is unaffected.

Starting November 9, participants will also receive a shareable Trading Identity card that reflects their trading habits, with a new card issued every Monday until the season ends.

“Bitbase 2.0 is about focus, and for our users, that means knowing their steady participation is recognized and credited,” said Nicholas Lo, Chief Business Officer at Bitbase. “That’s why ORIGIN started by crediting what users had already done with us. It doesn’t ask anyone to trade differently. It simply records the participation that’s already there, every day, for the next six months.”

Users can track their points and rankings in the Bitbase app and on the website. Full details are available at bitbase.com/points.

Bitbase is a digital asset exchange serving individual and institutional users worldwide, with products spanning Spot, Futures, TradFi and Earn. Bitbase aims to give users a stable and straightforward trading experience, in line with its brand statement, “Market Flows. We Focus.” Learn more at bitbase.com.

Une première pour un Français depuis 10 ans : Arthur Fils se qualifie pour les Finales ATP de Turin !

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026, Arthur Fils a validé mathématiquement sa qualification pour les Finales ATP de Turin, organisées du 15 au 22 novembre prochain. Le Français profite de l'exploit d'un autre Français, Quentin Halys, qui a éliminé Frances Tiafoe au Rolex Paris Masters.

Le dénouement s'est joué sur le court central de la Plénitude Arena à Nanterre. Opposé à l'Américain Frances Tiafoe, tête de série numéro 7 et 8e à la Race, Quentin Halys a signé une performance remarquable au deuxième tour du Rolex Paris Masters. Le 46e joueur mondial s'est imposé au terme d'un duel de 1 heure et 57 minutes (6-1, 3-6, 7-6 [9]). Frances Tiafoe servait pourtant pour le match à 5-4 dans la troisième manche, avant que Halys n'efface quatre balles de match dans le jeu décisif.

Un exploit retentissant. En se hissant en huitièmes de finale, Quentin Halys a précipité la fin des espoirs de l'Américain. En effet, ce revers de Frances Tiafoe valide définitivement la présence d'Arthur Fils à Turin parmi les huit meilleurs joueurs de la planète.

Cette qualification met fin à une longue attente pour le clan tricolore. Arthur Fils devient ainsi le premier joueur français à rallier les ATP Finals depuis Gaël Monfils en 2016. Une première depuis dix ans. À Turin, du 15 au 22 novembre 2026, il deviendra d'ailleurs le 10e joueur de l'histoire du tennis français à disputer ce prestigieux tournoi des maîtres de fin de saison.

La route menant Arthur Fils aux Finales ATP s'est révélée particulièrement atypique. En effet, le Français a manqué l'Open d'Australie et Roland-Garros en 2026 en raison de blessures, tout en restant discret à Wimbledon comme à l'US Open. Ainsi, il devient le premier joueur qualifié pour le Masters avec moins de deux matches gagnés en Grand Chelem sur une saison depuis Brad Gilbert en 1989.

Tête de série numéro 6, Arthur Fils dispute son deuxième tour du Rolex Paris Masters ce mercredi 4 novembre 2026 face à Tomas Machac, sur le court central, pas avant 20h30.

Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

It's time to finally do something about my dingy home office.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been through enough UK winters to know that things can get dark – and I don't just mean the incessant torment of existence (who's with me?!)

I mean working from home in a home office that is actually a spare room. And a spare room with crap light to boot. But there's a bit of tech for that, and over the last month or so I've been working with a SAD lamp right next to me. And it's had a massive positive impact on my day.

So I looked around and found the best SAD lamps from the best manufacturers in the US, all of which are on Amazon. As I explain below, you really can't go wrong with any of these, and as long as they're emitting 10,000 lux of brightness, you're only really paying more for the design and features of the lamp. For me, I really like the idea of having a magic pyramid on my desk!

This is the cheapest of the four SAD lamps here, but it absolutely does the job. It gives you the 10,000 lux that you need to smile, while also being a UV-free LED (which is standard). For $40, this is an easy recommendation.

With a more standard desk lamp aesthetic, the Halo lamp also offers wired and wireless phone charging features. I'm not the biggest fan of the design, but for $56, it's still a tempting bit of kit.

This is where the design of the SAD lamp comes into play – and the price tag goes UP! Foe me, this is definitely the most visually pleasing of all the four SAD lamps on the list. But then having a bit of futuristic ancient Egypt on hand is a bit of me.

The Clinical Light also boasts a striking design, and this and the Max version are both quite tall (18 and 22 inches). I feel like this might be too big to sit on your desk, but if you've got a spot for it to live, it will make you smile in return.

In a nutshell, SAD lamps mimic morning sunlight to balance internal body clocks. As their light enters our eyes it stimulates retinal cells. These cells then send signals to the brain to decrease melatonin (the sleepy hormone) and increase serotonin (the neurotransmitter that regulates happiness and energy). And this isn't all just vibes-based. Clinical trials confirm light therapy treats winter depression. I've had one for the last month, and I have absolutely felt the benefits.

For SAD lamps to be effective, they need to be able to pump out 10,000 lux of brightness from a normal sitting distances. All the lamps on this list achieve that. What's most interesting is that the more expensive lamps offer zero additional mood benefit. Budget boxes with certified output match luxury models, so you're just paying for design aesthetics and features (which admittedly are important).

A note on the light temperature – therapeutic lamps emit cool white light, so you won't be getting lovely honey-warm light with these. Blue wavelengths stimulate circadian photoreceptors in the retina. Warm white bulbs lack that blue spectrum and fail to trigger the internal wakefulness response, so keep that in mind before you click 'buy'.

Sir Terry Pratchett famously declared that cats remember when they were worshipped as gods, and it makes sense; our feline friends have an extra-special hold on our hearts – so much so that, yeah, we 100% want to know our birth month cat.

If you're one of those people who spends a lot of time reading up on how to make your yard more appealing to your cats (or which plants that are poisonous for cats) rather than tips on how to repel the neighborhood's kitties, then chances are you've wondered which cat breed best matches your personality at least once. At least.

It makes a lot of sense, too; after all, from playful kitties to lap cats that just want to be left alone to their sunbeam, there is an incredible amount of variety to be found in the feline kingdom. And after looking at our birth month pets, I couldn't resist taking a closer look at cats in particular...

I know, I know; we’re already familiar with the idea of a birth month bird, birth month animal, birth month owl, and birth month bug, but cats are particularly brilliant if you want to match a critter up with your personality.

Whether you're a determined January baby, a dreamy June soul or a fiercely independent November personality, there's a feline to match your character. And so, from adventurous Bengals to affectionate ragdolls, here are all 12 birth months matched to the cat breeds that best capture their personality traits.

Grab yourself a packet of catmint seeds, then, and get ready to find out which cat matches your birth month...

If you're a January baby, you're known for being ambitious, independent and determined. It should come as no surprise, then, that the Maine Coon is your birth month cat; after all, these striking kitties have a confident presence, are intelligent and have a reputation for being independent-minded.

A natural leader of the cat world? Sound about right!

February belongs to the Abyssinian, which makes a lot of sense when you think about it. Just like the creative, curious and intelligent people born at this time of year, Abyssinians are famously inquisitive, playful and adventurous.

In other words, these kitties are true free spirits. Sound familiar?

March babies are quiet, sensitive and introspective – but don't let the fact that they're not the loudest in the room fool you. Especially as their birth month cat is an elegant beauty who's often reserved around strangers but affectionate with their trusted people.

Basically, the Russian Blue is a perfect match for March's gentle and imaginative personality for a reason. And, if this has struck a nerve with you, then why not honor your birth month cat further with this Russian Blue Calendar 2027?

Bold, adventurous and full of charisma, April belongs to one of the more unusual members of the cat family: the Bengal. Unlike many cats that absolutely abhor water, these pretty kitties absolutely love it – almost as much as they love exploring. This, coupled with their energetic and confident natures, means they're not exactly known for sitting quietly on the sidelines! (Sound familiar?)

One of the most iconic cat breeds going, May's birth month cat is the sociable, expressive and strong-willed Siamese.

With their bright blue eyes and unusual coloring, these kitties are among the most instantly recognizable breeds in the US. They're also famously vocal and people-oriented, with plenty of personality to keep everyone entertained... just like May babies.

If you're a June baby, you're romantic, sensitive and affectionate. No surprises, then, that your birth month cat is the beautiful ragdoll! These gorgeous kitties are known for their gentle souls, their people-loving natures and their tendency to follow their favorite humans around the house.

Essentially, they're a lovely fit for June's dreamy and sentimental side. And they go all floppy like a ragdoll when you pick them up, making them excellent snugglers, too!

If you're a July baby, you're curious, private and quietly determined – and you tend to prefer a small but loyal friendship group to a big and sprawling one. Enter, then, one of the cutest birth month cats on this list: the Birman!

Loyal, loving and family-oriented. Birmans are often affectionate and sociable without being excessively demanding. They're the comforting presence of the feline family, basically, so lean into it!

Born in the height of summer, August babies tend to be every bit as sunny-natured as you think they'd be – think confident, outgoing and full of character. No wonder, then, that their birth month cat is the Burmese; these kitties are sociable, playful and love being involved in whatever their humans are doing.

They certainly know how to command attention, and all hail that kind of chaotic energy, quite frankly!

September's long been associated with successful leaders, which means those born under this month tend to be practical, composed and deeply intelligent. Their birth month cats are similar, as British Shorthairs are generally calm, independent and undemanding.

They appreciate a routine and like things just so, but they like it that way for a reason – and it's why they're one of the most popular cats around, as it makes for a cuddly and serene companion.

October babies, assemble! While some might expect those born in the spookiest month of all to be assigned a birth month cat like the hairless Sphynx cat, think again!

Turkish Angoras are intelligent, playful and often quite determined. They have a flair for the dramatic, too, making them an ideal match for passionate, expressive and sociable October-born folk everywhere. (Although, admittedly, this 'I Like A Handful Of Humans And My Turkish Angora' Mug is giving pure Scorpio energy!).

Wannabe witches, rejoice! November babies get the beautiful Bombay cat, which might be the most mysterious member of this list of birth month cats. Why? Well, because with their glossy black coats and striking eyes, these kitties have an enigmatic appearance, while often being deeply affectionate with their chosen people.

If this is your birth month cat, you're mysterious, intuitive and quietly determined... and a brilliant person to have in anyone's corner, quite frankly.

Last but not least, December babies are known for being adventurous, energetic and fun-loving – and generous of spirit enough to be able to deal with the fact that their birthday falls smack-bang in the middle of the holidays.

Somalis, then, make their ideal birth month cat, as they are curious, playful and love exploring their surroundings. (As an added bonus, they're simply stunning, too!).

Ernest Hemingway famously declared that “a cat has absolute emotional honesty: human beings, for one reason or another, may hide their feelings, but a cat does not.” Whichever birth month cat you call your own, then, try to follow its good example and be more in touch with your true feelings and self.

Remember, too, that you don't have to own a cat (does anybody truly own a cat, after all?) to enjoy seeing them in your garden; plant up some cat-friendly plants, and watch the kitties go to town. Just be sure to keep bird feeders up and out of their way, yeah?

The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

After two weeks without a conference, the justices return Friday to a relist lineup with a distinctly Southern accent. Four newly relisted cases come from Alabama. Three concern the same congressional district map and its seemingly inexhaustible capacity to generate Supreme Court litigation. The fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

The Supreme Court’s long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts is back for yet another round. Three related relists – Allen v. Milligan, Allen v. Singleton, and Allen v. Caster – ask the justices to revisit a congressional district map they have already considered several times. Readers may recall that in 2023, the court upheld a preliminary injunction against Alabama’s 2021 congressional map because the challengers were likely to succeed on their claim that it unlawfully diluted Black voting strength under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Alabama responded by drawing a new map that, like its predecessor, contained just one district in which Black voters had an opportunity to elect their preferred candidates.

After an 11-day trial, a three-judge district court found in 2025 that the replacement map violated both Section 2 and the 14th Amendment’s prohibition against intentional racial discrimination. But this spring, the Supreme Court changed the standards for Section 2 liability in Louisiana v. Callais and vacated the district court’s judgment for reconsideration. In the wake of that decision, the district court revisited the record and reached substantially the same conclusions that it had previously, issuing another preliminary injunction against the 2023 map. On June 2, the Supreme Court stayed that injunction, concluding that Alabama had shown a likelihood of success on the merits. That cleared the way for Alabama to use its preferred map in this week’s congressional elections.

Redistricting cases are among the rare types of cases over which the Supreme Court still has mandatory appellate jurisdiction. Alabama now seeks to appeal in Milligan and Singleton, and certiorari before judgment in Caster, the appeal of which is pending in the 11th Circuit. Alabama argues that the district court failed to follow Callais by disregarding the state’s legitimate redistricting priorities, particularly keeping Mobile and Baldwin Counties together as a Gulf Coast community of interest and protecting incumbents. It also contends that the district court wrongly attributed voting patterns to race rather than politics and failed to respect the presumption of legislative good faith. Alabama asks the justices to summarily reverse or, alternatively, take the cases for full review.

The challengers see things differently. They lead with mootness. In their motion to dismiss or affirm in Milligan, their motion to dismiss in Singleton, and their response in Caster, they argue that the injunction covers only the 2026 elections, which are underway using the 2023 plan, so that no live controversy remains. The Singleton plaintiffs note that the district court has scheduled trial for early 2027. Alabama responds that the injunction could continue to have legal effects, that election administration extends beyond Election Day, and that the requirement to use the court-drawn map may remain in force until Alabama adopts a new plan.

In Milligan and Caster, the challengers argue that the district court properly found the state’s asserted priorities were rationalizations for intentional discrimination. They point to legislators’ use of racial data, the removal of the city of Selma from Congressional District 2 “to ensure that Black voters there were ‘utterly unable to elect a representative of their choice,’” and unusual last-minute legislative findings “inserted into the bill on the morning of passage.” They maintain that Callais did not overrule the Supreme Court’s earlier Milligan decision and does not undermine the district court’s findings of intentional discrimination.

The justices’ June stay suggests that Alabama may have a receptive audience for its merits arguments. Whether the justices will reach those arguments – or conclude that no live controversy remains over the preliminary injunction – is less certain. Whatever happens, it seems unlikely that we’ve seen the last of Alabama’s congressional maps.

How can a car trip that never leaves Alabama become a matter of interstate commerce? That’s the question in Brown v. United States, which asks whether every automobile is automatically an “instrumentality of interstate commerce,” regardless of how it is used. The answer determines whether the federal government can prosecute a kidnapping committed entirely within one state based solely on the kidnapper’s use of a car.

In 2019, Derick Brown and her boyfriend abducted a three-year-old girl, driving her in Brown’s Toyota Sequoia from Birmingham to nearby Center Point, Alabama. The child was subsequently found dead. A federal jury convicted Brown of kidnapping (resulting in death) and conspiracy to kidnap, and she received a life sentence. The federal kidnapping statute, as amended in 2006, reaches kidnappings committed using “any means, facility, or instrumentality of interstate or foreign commerce.” Brown argued that using a car for a kidnapping committed entirely within Alabama, however, did not supply the interstate-commerce connection necessary for a federal prosecution. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit rejected Brown’s statutory and constitutional arguments, relying on its recent decision in United States v. Bryan holding that automobiles are per se instrumentalities of interstate commerce, even when used entirely within a single state.

Brown argues that the 11th Circuit’s rule would give Congress virtually unlimited authority over activities involving automobiles – potentially including everything from kidnapping to parking violations. More importantly for certiorari purposes, she identifies a circuit split. In United States v. Chavarria, she argues that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the proposition that motor vehicles are automatically instrumentalities of interstate commerce with regard to the federal kidnapping statute. Judge Victoria Calvert dissented in Bryan, warning that the majority had placed the 11th Circuit on the “wrong side of a developing split.” Georgetown law professor Randy Barnett and the Cato Institute filed amicus briefs supporting Brown, emphasizing the original limits of Congress’ commerce power.

The U.S. solicitor general responds that automobiles are instrumentalities of interstate commerce because they use highways, which are channels of interstate commerce, much as airplanes use airspace and railroad cars use railroads. Congress therefore may regulate their use even when the particular trip is entirely intrastate. The government also disputes the existence of a circuit split. It maintains that Chavarria held only that the broader category of “motor vehicles” – which can include lawnmowers, elevators, and motorized wheelchairs – is not invariably an instrumentality of interstate commerce. Brown calls that distinction “mere wordplay,” pointing out that the vehicle in Chavarria was a Jeep Cherokee, not a lawnmower.

We’ll be back next week to see whether the justices are ready to act – or whether these cases need another trip around the conference table.

Issue: Whether an automobile is per se an instrumentality of interstate commerce, which would make a federal offense of every kidnapping involving an automobile under 18 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1).

Issues:(1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

Issues: (1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

Issues: (1) Whether the district court erred by not requiring plaintiffs to offer an alternative map that performed just as well as the state’s map with respect to the state’s districting criteria; (2) whether the district court erred by finding racial-bloc voting without accounting for politics; (3) whether the district court erred by finding that the totality of circumstances suggests an objective likelihood of discrimination; and (4) whether the state violated the 14th Amendment by declining to draw a race-based plan.

Issue: Whether private instruction in courses required for state licensure constitutes government speech.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether, in a use-of-force case which involves multiple instances of force, Barnes v. Felix requires that each use-of-force be analyzed progressively from before the first instance of force used through the last instance of force used, considering the information known to the officer, the suspect’s prior actions (including any compliance, non-compliance, resistance, and reaching or grabbing for a weapon), and the suspect’s reactions to those prior use(s)-of-force, and, if so, whether Officers Moore and Kurtz violated Stephen Romero’s constitutional rights under this standard; and (2) whether, when analyzing a defendant law enforcement officer’s motion brought under Rule 12(b)(6) or 12(c), in a use-of-force case where body camera video clearly depicts the entire lead-up to and application of force by a law enforcement officer, the lower courts may analyze the clearly established prong of qualified immunity at a more general, plaintiff-friendly, level than at the motion for summary judgment stage of litigation and, if not, whether Officer Moore and Officer Kurtz are entitled to qualified immunity under the facts of this case.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

Issues: (1) Whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a violation of a clearly established constitutional right; and (2) whether a plaintiff can plead single-incident municipal liability without alleging a complete lack of training on the constitutional right in question.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the principles of Hope v. Pelzer are limited to Eighth Amendment claims or extend to free speech and free exercise clause claims such that petitioner’s constitutional claims should not be barred by qualified immunity.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

StandWithUs Center for Legal Justice v. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 25-1404

Issues: (1) Whether the harassers’ subjective discriminatory intent is an element of a hostile environment claim under Title VI; and (2) whether the First Amendment bars a plaintiff from pleading a Title VI hostile environment claim based on “protected speech.”

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

Issue: Whether, and under what circumstances, a bankruptcy court may override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor a valid arbitration agreement with respect to Section 362(k) claims.

(Relisted after the Sept. 28, Oct. 9, and Oct. 16 conferences.)

Issue: Whether the law clearly established that the officer’s use of a less-lethal projectile, under the totality of the circumstances, constituted an unreasonable use of force in violation of the Fourth Amendment.

(Relisted after the Oct. 9 and 16 conferences.)

Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia, 25-1426

Issues: (1) Whether the Fifth Amendment exempts intangible property from the per se rules that govern takings of tangible property; and (2) whether Puerto Rico enjoys any form of immunity from suit in federal court and, if so, whether the Lanham Act abrogates that immunity.

(Relisted after the Oct. 9 and 16 conferences.)

John P. Elwood is a partner at Arnold & Porter in Washington, D.C., specializing in appellate litigation and administrative law.

CommonSpirit Health has locked in a deal to sell three hospitals to Altru Health System, rural North Dakota nonprofit.

The deal is contingent on regulatory review and other customary closing conditions, but expected to close in early 2027. The pair's new definitive agreement, announced Wednesday, follows 10 months of due diligence following a letter of intent unveiled near the top of the year (see that story below). Financial details were not disclosed.

The to-be-sold facilities are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison.

They would join Altru's flagship acute care hospital, a critical access hospital it also purchased from CommonSpirit in March, a trauma center, a specialty hospital and 20 practices spread across the northern part of the state.

The organizations said there are no changes to patient care or day-to-day operations related to the deal. The hospitals will maintain their Catholic identity and mission.

"Through our work together over the years, we’ve developed tremendous confidence in Altru’s commitment to high-quality, compassionate care," Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health's Central Region, said in reference to prior partnerships with the  We believe Altru is the right partner to build on St. Alexius’ proud legacy, honor its Catholic mission and continue serving patients and families for generations to come.”

CommonSpirit is in the midst of a sweeping operational overhaul as it looks to bolster its financial performance ahead of imminent Medicaid cuts. Those efforts have opened the $42.4 billion system to a string of hospital divestitures, including its four handoffs to Altru as well as the sale of a four-hospital Ohio system to UPMC in September.

CommonSpirit Health and Altru Health System are considering a deal to transfer three North Dakota hospitals to the latter, the organizations announced Thursday.

The pair’s signed letter of intent outlines plans to evaluate a potential deal for the facilities, a process they said would run “the next several months” before a potential definitive agreement might be struck.

In the balance are CHI St. Alexius Health Bismarck, a multispecialty acute care medical center in the state’s capital, and two smaller critical access hospitals, CHI St. Alexius Health Turtle Lake and CHI St. Alexius Health Garrison. All three are Catholic facilities within CommonSpirit’s regional healthcare system CHI St. Alexius Health.

Potential financial terms of any deal for the hospitals were not disclosed, nor were any details on whether other assets tied to the hospitals, such as clinics, would be included.

“This is a natural next step in exploring how we can continue to support strong, sustainable healthcare for the region,” Tim Bricker, president of CommonSpirit Health’s central region, which includes CHI St. Alexius Health, said in the announcement.

CommonSpirit is a $40 billion nonprofit that counted 137 hospitals in two dozen states. It’s in the midst of an operating performance turnaround initiative and, at this month’s J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference, teased “a couple” of portfolio divestitures to be announced in the next quarter as part of the effort.

Grand Forks, North Dakota-based Altru Health System is a smaller nonprofit, with just over $700 million of revenue in 2024 from its sole acute care hospital, a specialty hospital and 20 practice locations in northeast North Dakota and northwest Minnesota. It opened a new $500 million hospital in January 2025.

The news comes hot on the heels of another deal between the systems for ownership of CHI St. Alexius Health Devils Lake, another critical access hospital. That handoff was unveiled in December and is set to close March 1.

Both deals have been described as a boon for rural communities and an opportunity for Altru to better coordinate its local care.

“Altru has a long history of serving communities across North Dakota and northwest Minnesota, and our organizations share a deep respect for the people we serve and the responsibility that comes with delivering local healthcare,” Todd Forkel, CEO of Altru, said in the announcement. “We look forward to working more closely with CommonSpirit to strengthen access to care for patients and families well into the future.”

The Unproven Economics of the Weekend Cruise

📅 2026-11-04  |  Read Source →

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Cruise lines are moving some of their biggest ships onto shorter trips. Grok

Cruise lines are putting some of their biggest ships on shorter trips, but the financial evidence that those voyages generate better returns remains thin.

Cruise lines are moving some of their biggest ships onto three- and four-night trips, betting that shorter vacations will bring customers back more often. But more passengers are not the same as more profit. Norwegian shortened its average cruise this year, carried 24% more guests, and earned less revenue and gross margin per passenger-day. That does not prove short cruises are bad business, but it does mean the weekend math needs more scrutiny.

For decades, the industry sold seven-night vacations. As ships grew larger and added water parks, more restaurants, and bigger shows, short sailings went to older, smaller ships that sold for less.

Disney was already doing this with the Wish in 2022, and Virgin Voyages launched its first ship on four- and five-night Caribbean itineraries in 2021.

Cruise lines are putting their newest and largest ships on three- and four-night itineraries, a break from the seven-night template the industry built its economics around. Royal Caribbean started it at megaship scale with Utopia of the Seas from Port Canaveral in 2024, and Carnival will follow with Mardi Gras on four- and five-day Bahamas sailings from the same port in May 2027. The logic is frequency: a ship running alternating short trips serves two sets of guests a week instead of one, doubling embarkations and the chance to sell drink packages, specialty dining, and excursions. Royal Caribbean Group CEO Jason Liberty said on the October 27 earnings call that half of the group's guests are millennials or younger, that they spend about as much on a short trip as on a seven-night cruise, and that onboard spending has beaten expectations. The filings are harder to read. Royal Caribbean's revenue per passenger-day rose only to about $320 from $315 in the first nine months of 2026, with ticket revenue per passenger-day flat, and its average voyage barely shortened, from 6.2 days to 6.1. Norwegian, which has cut its average cruise from about 8.6 days to 7.5, carried 24% more passengers but saw revenue per passenger-day fall from $401 to $385 and gross margin per passenger-day drop nearly 11%. Neither company reports results by cruise length, so the weekend model's profitability cannot be verified from public disclosures.

Eastbourne Borough claimed three valuable Isthmian Premier points on Tuesday night with a 1-0 victory over lowly Stanway Rovers – but for manager Steve King, it was all about the elements as well as the opposition.

The Sports extended their incredible current run to 14 victories in 15 starts – just the 3-0 FA Cup defeat at Salisbury blotching the record – as they swept aside second-bottom Stanway Rovers at the Connect Management Stadium.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Skipper Josh Rees notched the crucial goal just before half-time, and Borough spurned a whole clutch of chances to make the game safe against gritty opposition, in front of a huddled crowd of 619 – only a little over one-third of Saturday's attendance against Ramsgate.

The victory nudges the Sports up to third in the table, ahead of a potentially difficult trip to Dartford on Saturday.

Borough are, frankly, the team to beat right now, as this compelling campaign moves towards the winter. But for the players, supporters and the gaffer himself, Tuesday night was no feast of football, just a test of endurance.

"Shocking! Not my team, nor even the opposition, but the weather! If you don't know Eastbourne, you don't know our weather. It was horrendous - the wind especially - it's the worst I've ever seen it - and I live in this town!" said King.

"It was appalling and it ruined the game - no flow or pattern. It was just a match that you wanted to be finished, as soon as the referee blew his first whistle.

"But ultimately you just go about your business. Sometimes if you can 'win horribly' like that, it is actually a good sign. We can't always play great football and win. Long throws, headers off the line, you just do what you have to.

"But we did miss five unbelievable chances, and I mean five, to make the game safe. Their keeper has made three or four brilliant saves - but we should be putting those chances to bed.

"Poor as the game was, poor as the conditions were, we've had chances and we should have taken and made the game safe. So I was disappointed from that point of view, but… cross it off, game done. You can only get three points for a win, whatever the quality or the conditions or the opposition."

Is King: the new Michael Fish? Readers of a certain age will just still remember the infamous forecast in 1987 from the BBC weatherman - the night before a hurricane swept across southern England. Michael actually lived in Eastbourne: perhaps he should have known better.

There was no football stadium at Priory Lane back then, but the flat Langney landscape has always been open to all the elements. Never mind, you hardy Borough fans: not even the worst that the Channel throws at us can blow King's Sports off course.
